procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 7th August, 1952, of the High Court of Judicature, for the State of Punjab at Simla in Criminal Revision No. 78 of 1952
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The District Magistrate, Jullundur, reported the case for revision of the Order. A single Judge referred the case for decision by a Division Bench due to diversity of judicial opinion. The Division Bench accepted the respondent's contention and set aside the conviction and sentence imposed under section 7 of the Act.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of Punjab appealed to the Supreme Court after the High Court set aside the conviction. The appeal was brought under Article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution of India, based on a certificate granted by the High Court.

decision.conviction_status: The conviction by the trying Magistrate is upheld.
decision.sentence_status: The sentence passed by the trying Magistrate shall stand.
directions: The judgment of the High Court is set aside.
It is unnecessary for the High Court to hear the reference made to it by the District Magistrate, Jullundur any further.
The sentence already passed upon the respondent by the trying Magistrate shall stand and if the fine of Rs. 120 has not already been paid, it shall be paid now.
In default, the respondent shall suffer rigorous imprisonment for one month.

issue.issue_text: Whether a criminal liability incurred under a repealed Ordinance continues after its repeal and the enactment of a new Act, especially when the new Act's saving provisions do not explicitly preserve such liability.

facts: An individual committed a criminal offense under a temporary Ordinance.
Before the legal proceedings were concluded, the Ordinance was repealed and replaced by a new Act.
The saving provisions in the new Act did not explicitly state that criminal liabilities incurred under the old Ordinance would continue after its repeal.
law: The Supreme Court centered its decision on Section 6 of the General Clauses Act.
This Act provides a default rule that the repeal of an enactment does not affect any liability, penalty, or punishment incurred under the repealed law.
This rule applies to all repeals unless the new repealing statute shows a "different intention."
application: The Court rejected the High Court's argument that Section 6 of the General Clauses Act only applies to a "simple repeal" (where no new law is enacted) and not to a "repeal and re-enactment."
It held that Section 6 applies in all cases of repeal, including when a new law simultaneously replaces the old one.
The Court clarified that the correct legal test is not whether the new Act positively keeps the old liabilities alive, but whether it shows an intention that is inconsistent with their continuation.

The Court found that the new Act did not express any intention inconsistent with the survival of the liability incurred under the old Ordinance. The absence of a specific saving clause was considered immaterial.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the criminal liability incurred under the repealed Ordinance continued to exist. This was because Section 6 of the General Clauses Act applied by default, and the new Act did not demonstrate a "different intention" to extinguish such pre-existing liabilities.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 6 of the General Clauses Act is ruled out when there is a repeal of an enactment followed by a fresh legislation which contains its own saving provisions.

facts: The case involved an offense committed under a temporary Ordinance.
This Ordinance was subsequently repealed and replaced by a new Act before the Ordinance's natural expiration date.
The High Court held that the liability for the offense under the old Ordinance was extinguished because the new Act did not contain a provision to save it.
law: Section 6 of the General Clauses Act provides that when an enactment is repealed, the repeal shall not affect any liability or penalty incurred under the repealed enactment, unless a 'different intention appears' in the new legislation.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's view that Section 6 applies only to a 'simple repeal' (where no new law is enacted) and not to a repeal followed by a fresh enactment.
The Court established that whenever there is a repeal, the consequences laid down in Section 6 will follow, unless the new legislation shows a 'different intention'.
The correct 'line of enquiry' is not whether the new Act expressly keeps old liabilities alive, but whether it manifests an intention to destroy them.
The Court clarified that an intention to destroy old liabilities must be incompatible with or contrary to the provisions of Section 6.

This incompatibility must be ascertained from all the provisions of the new law, and the mere absence of a saving clause is not, by itself, material or sufficient to indicate such a contrary intention.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition, holding that Section 6 of the General Clauses Act is not automatically ruled out when a repeal is followed by fresh legislation. It applies in such cases unless the new legislation, when viewed as a whole, manifests a clear and incompatible intention to destroy the rights and liabilities that existed under the repealed law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the correct line of enquiry is to see if the new enactment expressly keeps alive old rights and liabilities, or if it manifests an intention to destroy them.

facts: The case involves the question of whether a criminal liability incurred under a repealed law (an Ordinance) continues to exist after a new law (an Act) replaces it.
The new Act did not contain an explicit saving clause that preserved the criminal liability from the old Ordinance.
law: The Court's analysis is based on Section 6 of the General Clauses Act.
Section 6 states that the repeal of an enactment shall not affect any right, liability, or punishment incurred under the repealed law, unless a "different intention appears" in the new legislation.
application: The Court rejected the view that one must look for a provision in the new law that "positively kept alive" the rights and liabilities from the repealed law. It called this an "erroneous and incorrect approach."
The Court clarified that the absence of a specific saving clause in the new law is "neither material nor decisive."

Instead, the Court established the correct legal test: "The line of enquiry would be, not whether the new Act expressly keeps alive old rights and liabilities but whether it manifests an intention to destroy them."
This means that Section 6 of the General Clauses Act is the default rule, even when a repeal is followed by new legislation. The rights and liabilities from the old law are presumed to survive.
To overcome this presumption, the new legislation must show an intention that is "incompatible with or contrary to" the provisions of Section 6.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the issue, concluding that the correct line of inquiry is to determine if the new enactment manifests an intention to destroy old rights and liabilities, not whether it contains an express provision to keep them alive. The default position under Section 6 of the General Clauses Act is that such rights and liabilities survive the repeal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a criminal liability incurred under a repealed Ordinance continues after its repeal and the enactment of a new Act, especially when the new Act's saving provisions do not explicitly preserve such liability.
appellant_arguments: The criminal liability continues to exist because the consequences of a repeal, as laid down in Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, will follow unless the new Act shows a 'different intention'.
The new Act does not manifest an intention to destroy the liability incurred under the old Ordinance, therefore the liability is preserved by the general law.
respondent_arguments: The liability does not continue because the new Act, which replaced the Ordinance, has its own saving provisions, and these provisions do not explicitly preserve the liability for an offense committed under the repealed Ordinance.
Since the new legislation does not deal with the matter of old offenses, it should be presumed that the Legislature did not deem it fit to keep alive the liability incurred under the old Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 6 of the General Clauses Act is ruled out when there is a repeal of an enactment followed by a fresh legislation which contains its own saving provisions.
appellant_arguments: Section 6 of the General Clauses Act is not ruled out. Its provisions apply automatically upon repeal unless the new legislation shows a 'different intention'.
The mere presence of some saving clauses in the new Act does not, by itself, constitute a 'different intention' that would exclude the general application of Section 6.
respondent_arguments: Section 6 is ruled out because there has been a fresh legislation on the subject.

When a new Act is passed, it cannot be presumed that the legislature inadvertently omitted a provision to save old liabilities; rather, if the new Act is silent on the matter, it is presumed the legislature did not intend to keep the liability alive, thereby displacing the general rule in Section 6.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the correct line of enquiry is to see if the new enactment expressly keeps alive old rights and liabilities, or if it manifests an intention to destroy them.
appellant_arguments: The correct line of enquiry is to determine if the new enactment manifests an intention to destroy the rights and liabilities that existed under the repealed law.
The default position is that old liabilities are preserved by Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, and they continue unless actively nullified by the new law.
respondent_arguments: The correct approach is to see if the new enactment has provisions that positively and expressly keep alive the rights and liabilities from the repealed law.
If the new Act's saving provisions do not explicitly preserve a specific liability, that liability is extinguished.

statutes.act_name: The new Act that replaced the Ordinance (unnamed in text)

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Whenever an enactment is repealed, the consequences laid down in section 6 of the General Clauses Act will follow unless the new enactment shows a different intention. This rule applies even when a repeal is followed by a simultaneous re-enactment. A contrary intention is determined by examining if the new enactment's provisions put an end to rights and liabilities under the repealed law; the absence of a specific saving clause in the new law is not decisive.
obiter: The expression 'anything done' in a saving clause does not include an act done by a person in contravention of the provisions of the repealed law.

Judicial opinion in America regarding simultaneous repeal and re-enactment, where the re-enactment is considered a reaffirmation of the old law, is not uniform and the court expressed no opinion on it.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Whenever there is a repeal of an enactment, the consequences laid down in section 6 of the General Clauses Act will follow unless a different intention appears in the new legislation. This principle applies even when the repeal is followed by a simultaneous re-enactment. The correct approach is not to search for a positive provision in the new law that keeps old liabilities alive, but rather to determine if the new law manifests a clear intention to destroy the rights and liabilities that accrued under the repealed law. The absence of a specific saving clause in the new enactment preserving old liabilities is neither material nor decisive.
legal_tests_applied: Upon the repeal of an enactment, the consequences specified in Section 6 of the General Clauses Act automatically follow, unless the repealing act shows a 'different intention'.

To ascertain if a 'different intention' exists, the correct line of enquiry is to examine the new enactment to see whether it has put an end to the rights and liabilities that existed under the repealed law.
It is an erroneous and incorrect approach to enquire if the new enactment has by its provisions positively and expressly kept alive the rights and liabilities from the repealed law.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning presumes that a legislature does not intend to allow offenders to escape liability due to a technicality when a law is repealed and re-enacted. This prevents the inadvertent creation of a legal loophole.

The default application of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act promotes legal continuity and stability, ensuring that rights and liabilities persist through legislative updates unless the legislature makes a conscious and explicit decision to extinguish them.
